question: The efficacy of oral rehydration solution (ORS) in secretory diarrhoea depends critically on which intestinal transporter?

answers.text: The sodium-glucose co-transporter (SGLT1) in the small intestinal enterocyte, which couples glucose absorption to sodium — and therefore water — uptake

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. SGLT1 couples sodium and glucose absorption and remains functional even during cholera toxin-induced chloride hypersecretion. ORS exploits this transporter: glucose drives sodium absorption, water follows osmotically, and net fluid absorption is restored.

answers.text: The CFTR chloride channel, which is inhibited by glucose to reduce fluid secretion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. CFTR is a chloride channel stimulated (not inhibited) by cAMP — cholera toxin acts by locking CFTR open via cAMP. Glucose has no direct inhibitory effect on CFTR. ORS works around CFTR dysfunction, not through it.

answers.text: The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase proton pump in the large intestine, which absorbs potassium while excreting acid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the gastric acid pump; it is not the mechanism by which ORS promotes intestinal water absorption. Its role in colonic potassium conservation is also unrelated to the SGLT1-based ORS mechanism.

answers.text: Aquaporin-3 channels, which are directly upregulated by the glucose in ORS to increase water reabsorption

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While aquaporins facilitate transcellular water movement, ORS efficacy is governed by the sodium-glucose co-transporter that creates the osmotic gradient — aquaporin upregulation by glucose in ORS is not the pharmacological basis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Revisit the ORS section. The key insight is that cholera toxin selectively disables one sodium transporter but leaves SGLT1 (the sodium-glucose co-transporter) intact — and ORS is specifically designed to exploit this residual transporter.

Excellent. The SGLT1 mechanism is why ORS works even in cholera: the toxin blocks NaCl co-transport but cannot block sodium-glucose co-transport — glucose in ORS 'rescues' sodium and water absorption through a different channel.
